claims.value: Side A attacked. claims.rationale: Both sides' sources describe the French attacking side B's bridges and positions; side B's counter-strokes were made inside its own position, so they do not make it the attacker. claims.value: In side A's accounts side B attacked. Dupont's division, ordered to surround Ulm, could not carry out the order and had only time to prepare for battle at Haslach: the enemy decided its movement on the spot, its artillery playing on the front of the French position while several infantry columns preceded by many squadrons came on against the French right and it deployed out of its entrenchments on the French left. Alombert and Colin say the division had been established at Haslach only a short time, its posts just placed, when the enemy attacked, and Dupont's later letter has the Archduke detach a large corps to attack him. The French bayonet charges and the fight for Jungingen, on which the French right rested, were made against these attacks.
claims.rationale: Coded from Dupont's division journal (read from the page image), his later letter and the French official history: side B took the offensive and Dupont accepted battle at Haslach; his charges were counterattacks from his position, which by the brief's rule do not make side A the attacker. Dupont's orders were to invest Ulm, but these accounts say he could not begin to carry them out. The accounts show side B's attack decided on the field ('décidé sur-le-champ'; the Archduke in Dupont's letter), so the posture is tagged commander_created; who in side B's command decided it is disputed (claim side-b-decisions). Krauss's account, coded separately, has the French attack first (claim posture-krauss). The Jungingen passage is from Titeux's account drawn from Dupont's manuscript memoirs, which Alombert and Colin quote in a note. English renderings (ours): 'the general had orders to surround Ulm, resting his right on the Blau'; 'he cannot carry out this order, he has only time to prepare for battle'; 'the enemy's movement is decided on the spot; while his artillery plays on the front of our position, he carries several columns of infantry preceded by a great number of squadrons against our right. He also deploys out of his entrenchments on our left'; 'the division had been established at Haslach only a short time, its posts had just been placed, when the enemy attacked'; 'as soon as the Archduke sees that our movement has been halted at the sight of his order of battle, he detaches from his position a large corps of infantry and cavalry to attack us'; '[Jungingen,] on which our right rests, and whose possession is indispensable to us'.

claims.value: In Krauss's account side A attacked first and side B attacked on another part of the field. Dupont's division drove in the Austrian outposts at Haslach, threw back the battalions of the regiment Riese sent to support them and continued its attack against the Austrian right wing as far as Böfingen; after the fight on the southern wing had begun, Austrian troops were sent forward via Jungingen, apparently to envelop the French right, and Dupont decided to forestall that attack. Krauss calls the action the attack of Dupont's division, and quotes Mack's report that the French attacked the army's right wing with great violence while Mack led a considerable part of the left wing into the rear of the enemy right.
claims.rationale: Coded from Krauss's narrative and the Austrian report he quotes: main attacks by each side on different parts of the field, so both_attacked. Dupont's attack followed Ney's order to invest Ulm, which Krauss calls clear but impracticable, and the passages show Dupont deciding to forestall the Austrian attack; the Austrian envelopment was decided on the field, by Schwarzenberg according to the Archduke and by Mack according to Mack's relation (claim side-b-decisions). Both attacks were decided at this engagement, so the posture is tagged commander_created. Krauss also says Mack contented himself with fending off the enemy (claim side-b-objectives), and the French accounts are coded separately (claim posture-french-accounts). The hour in the OCR is not restated. English renderings (ours): 'the division came upon the enemy outposts at Haslach, which were driven back'; 'these, however, were thrown back by the French, who now continued their attack against the Austrian right wing as far as Böfingen'; 'at the time when the fight on the southern wing had already begun, Austrian troops were directed forward over Jungingen, apparently to envelop the French right wing'; 'decided to forestall this attack'; 'under these circumstances the attack of Dupont's division took place on 11 October at ... in the afternoon'; Mack, 'that the army was attacked at midday on the 11th before Ulm by the French army of observation under Ney on its right wing with great violence'; '"our right wing repulsed all attacks with great steadfastness, while the quartermaster general FML Mack had a considerable part of our left wing advance and led it into the rear of the enemy right'.

claims.value: In side A's accounts side B's artillery fought from works: the 6th corps journal says that when the 1st division reached Haslach the enemy brought the artillery of his entrenchments into play against it and deployed considerable forces in high works on the Spitzberg, and Dupont's report that at nightfall the enemy went back into his entrenchments; Dupont's journal has the enemy deploy out of his entrenchments on the French left. Side A held the village of Haslach, the ground toward Jungingen and the woods with no works named; Ney had told Dupont to keep his posts well entrenched and covered by abatis, but his posts had just been placed when the enemy attacked.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified because cited passages have side B's artillery fire on the division from its entrenchments; its infantry and cavalry fought in front of them, so the works covered only part of side B's force. The passages do not say who built the works or when: the Emperor's order to Ney to take Ulm mentions works the Austrians had begun there, and Krauss says Colonel Bianchi inspected the entrenchments on the morning of the 11th, so the phase is unresolved. Krauss's account is coded separately (claim fortification-krauss). English renderings (ours): 'the enemy brought the artillery of his entrenchments into play against the division and deployed in high works on the Spitzberg hill considerable forces'; 'the enemy went back into his entrenchments (and behind)'; 'he also deploys out of his entrenchments on our left'; 'to finish the works that the Austrians have begun'; Krauss, 'Colonel Bianchi, who on the morning of the 11th had inspected the entrenchments and the positions of the troops'; 'your posts well entrenched and covered with abatis'; 'its posts had just been placed when the enemy attacked'; 'Colonel Darrieau with a battalion of the 32nd held the position of Haslach'.

claims.value: Both sides fought from works. Side B: the Archduke had a line of entrenchments built on Campagnola 1,000 m from Castel Vecchio, a closed redoubt and three flèches with a demi-lune (Koch), or a redoubt about 1200 paces from the castle and three flèches among the foremost houses (Angeli); Veronetta had a bastioned enceinte flanked by towers, partly demolished, and two dismantled old forts (Koch); its bridges were closed by tambours, each with 1 gun, and a crenellated wall covered the passage along the bank (Angeli). Duhesme's report has side A take the enemy redoubts with their guns, force the entrenched posts and loopholed houses, and meet flanking fire from the fortifications of S. Giorgio; Angeli has the fire of the works check side A and the redoubt hold out until surrounded. Side A: its guns fired from Castel Vecchio, flanked by four towers with ditches, whose front facing Austria had recently been put in a state of defence, and from the intact bastion of Spain, whose heavy guns swept the left bank (Koch); Angeli says side A held its ground only with the help of the superior fire from the fortress. The bridges were barricaded at both ends (Koch).
claims.rationale: Koch, Duhesme and Angeli agree on the works, so they are recorded in one claim (page images, except the passages marked OCR). Side A's part is its artillery in the castle and on the bastion, while its infantry attacked in the open; side B's infantry fought from the works and Veronetta. The permanent works (the castle, the bastion, Veronetta's walls and forts) are inherited, while the Campagnola works were built on the Archduke's orders before the action, not by side B's commander at this engagement, so the claim is tagged unresolved, as for B365a. Angeli's footnote says the Archduke had ordered these works not to be occupied (claim side-b-objectives), yet both accounts have them manned. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'but foreseeing the advantage we could draw from it, Archduke Charles had had raised there, 1,000 metres from Castel Vecchio, a line of entrenchments consisting of a closed redoubt at Artaglia and of three flèches thrown up between the houses of the suburb and the enceinte of Veronetta, with a demi-lune to defend their front and flanks'; Angeli, 'the suburb of S. claims.value: Both sides attacked. Side A opened the battle: on the 29th Seras crossed the Adige above Verona, Duhesme and Gardanne crossed at Castel Vecchio against the Austrian troops in the hills, the other divisions forced the Austrian advanced guard at S. Michele back on the position, and Molitor attacked the advanced troops before the position, side A establishing itself in Strà and even Caldiero at dusk; on the 30th it attacked Colognola, Caldiero and the Austrian left at Gombione and Sabbionara, and on the 31st Verdier and Duhesme attacked the Austrian left up to the works of Chiavicca del Christo. Side B attacked on the 30th: the Archduke had resolved to break out of his position and throw side A back over the Adige, and his plan was a thrust from both wings with the main attack, which he meant to lead himself, toward Caldiero and Vago; when firing began on his left he attacked, and Bellegarde's column advanced along the chaussée and forced side A out of Strà. Koch says the Archduke sent four columns out of the entrenchments to threaten side A's flanks and ease the advance of his centre on the chaussée.
claims.rationale: Both accounts describe main attacks by each side on the 30th, so the code is both_attacked; side B's attack of the 30th was planned as a sortie to throw side A back over the Adige, not a counterattack inside its position. The counterattacks at Colognola and by Hohenlohe's grenadiers were inside the position and do not by themselves make side B an attacker. Angeli also writes that the French were everywhere the attackers and that in each decisive action the Austrians fought a superior attacker (claims side-a-losses-reported and angeli-side-a); this is kept in the record. Both commanders at the battle decided to attack (claims side-a-command and side-b-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created, although Koch says the offensive was forbidden the Archduke from above. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'but Prince Charles changed his plan and sent four columns out of the entrenchments to threaten our flanks and ease the march of his centre on the chaussée'; Angeli, 'by Archduke Charles's plan a simultaneous rapid thrust from both wings was to threaten the enemy's flanks and ease the main attack, which he himself meant to lead in the direction Caldiero-Vago'; 'driving the enemy skirmishers before him, he forced the evacuation of the village' (OCR); Koch, 'Count Bellegarde, driving before it the skirmishers of the division Gardanne' (OCR) 'was advancing majestically, closed in mass, and forcing the centre of that division to give ground as far as the Rotta' (OCR); Angeli, 'on the ... (OCR) at daybreak the divisions Duhesme and Gardanne passed the bridge at Castel Vecchio and pushed the outposts back on their supports' (OCR); 'at noon the divisions Espagne, Mermet, Molitor and Partonneaux crossed the quickly repaired bridges and drew up before the Porta del Vescovo on the road to Vicenza' (OCR); 'GM Frimont, who commanded the advanced guard of the Austrian right wing at S. Michele, held out bravely against superior numbers for several hours' (OCR) 'and only toward ... (OCR) in the afternoon ... went back step by step by S. Martino to the position of Caldiero' (OCR); 'the villages of Vago, Ca dell'Ara and Strà were taken and lost several times, until at last, as dusk began, the French succeeded in establishing themselves in Strà and even in Caldiero' (OCR); Koch, 'Verdier set out on the morning of the 31st'; and as in claims side-a-command and side-b-command.

claims.value: Side B fought from an entrenched position. Angeli calls it a position strengthened alike by nature and art, and says the Archduke had, since his arrival in Italy, raised its natural strength by extensive entrenchments: redoubts crowned the most important points of the right wing, trenches and advanced breastworks covered the slopes the redoubts could not sweep, the church and village of Colognola were prepared for defence, and on the left there were redoubts at Chiavigetto and Chiavicca del Christo and armed flèches at Ponterotto and Belfiore di Porcile, with firing steps for infantry cut in the dykes along the Adige and the Alpone; a Grenzer battalion held the work at Ponte Zerpa. Koch describes a redoubt on Monte Nafari, redoubts sweeping the Verona road and the plain of Caldiero, the church of Colognola surrounded by a good wall, a flèche at Chiavighetto and a redoubt near Ponte Ratto, a strong redoubt at Chiavica del Cristo and all houses fit for defence entrenched, and the centre in the entrenchments of Ponterotto. Side A attacked these works: on the 29th it pushed up to the trenches and was thrown back by fire from the works (Angeli); on the 30th some of its soldiers got in by the embrasures of a redoubt at Colognola and a regiment's eagles waved for a moment on the parapet before the defenders remained masters of the work (Koch); on the 31st side A advanced to the foot of the entrenchments and assailed them (Koch), and Nordmann threw part of his brigade into the redoubt at Chiavicca del Christo (Angeli). No passage read places side A in works.
claims.rationale: Koch and Angeli agree on the works, so they are recorded in one claim (OCR except Koch's pp. 94, 97 and 104 and Angeli's p. 115, read from the page images; counts of works, guns and men and regiment numbers seen only in the OCR are not restated). They are field works which, Angeli says, the Archduke, side B's commander at this battle, had laid out for this position, and Koch says he chose the entrenched position to receive the battle, so the claim is tagged commander_created; Angeli says the Archduke had given the position his greatest care since his arrival in Italy, and the passages read give no dates for the works. English renderings (ours): Angeli, 'in possession of an excellently chosen position, strengthened equally by nature and art' (OCR); 'to this position, which commands the whole Adige from Verona to the mouth of the Alpone, Archduke Charles had since his arrival in Italy, with wise foresight, given the greatest care, and had further increased its natural strength by laying out extensive entrenchments' (OCR); 'redoubts crowned the most important points of the right wing' (OCR); 'was remedied by trenches and advanced breastworks, which at the same time gave the infantry valuable cover' (OCR); 'the church of Colognola, as well as the village lying partly on the height, partly on the slope, were prepared for defence' (OCR); 'on the left wing of the position there were redoubts at Chiavigetto and Chiavicca del Christo, then armed flèches at Ponterotto and Belfiore di Porcile to sweep the roads coming from Gombioni and Madonna di Strà' (OCR); 'besides, firing steps for infantry were also cut in the dykes along the Adige and the Alpone' (OCR); '1 battalion of Grenzer held the work of Ponte Zerpa'; Koch, 'Monte Nafari, the extreme and highest point of the right, was protected by a redoubt armed with ... (OCR) cannon and a howitzer' (OCR); '... (OCR) redoubts had been added to these entrenchments to sweep the Verona chaussée and the plain of Caldiero' (OCR); 'the steepest slope of the spur descends from Monte Nafari to Colognola, whose church is surrounded by a good wall' (OCR); 'a flèche at Chiavighetto covered the first, and a redoubt near Ponte Ratto defended the second. A strong redoubt supported the left at Chiavica del Cristo, and besides these works all the houses fit for defence had been entrenched'; the centre 'in the entrenchments of Ponterotto' as in claim koch-side-b; Angeli, 'they pushed with commendable bravery up to the trenches of the position' (OCR), 'where the cool bravery of the infantry regiment Lindenau and a murderous fire of guns and muskets from the works of the position threw them back on Caldiero' (OCR); Koch, 'some soldiers of the ... (OCR) manage to get in through the embrasures as the guns recoil, and the eagles of this regiment wave for a moment on the parapet' (OCR); 'and leave the defenders masters of the work' (OCR); 'Nordmann, believing he could bar his way, sent a strong detachment out of the entrenchments to meet him. After a lively engagement at Gombione, where this general fell badly wounded, the Austrians were repulsed, and our troops advanced to the foot of the entrenchments, which they assailed'; Angeli, 'the Austrian general had to fall back on Chiavicca del Christo after long resistance' (OCR); 'he threw himself with part of it into the redoubt' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A attacked. In Koch, Charpentier had Hillinger attacked at once by the 22nd, which was thrown back; Solignac, sent to envelop Hillinger, attacked when the new summons was refused, supported by dragoons and cuirassiers, and Hillinger capitulated. In Angeli, Hillinger awaited the attack on 2 November standing fast and repulsed it, and after he refused a second summons 8 battalions and 14 squadrons advanced to the attack from all sides. Side B's earlier advance to the heights of Fojano (Angeli) and on Ca Albertini (Koch) was the demonstration against Veronetta it had been ordered to make.
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side A attack Hillinger's brigade, and Angeli says the brigade awaited the attack standing fast, so the code is A_attacked. Side B's advance was a demonstration ordered from above, and no passage read has it attack side A's positions; in Koch the 22nd attacked it and was thrown back onto the château's breaches. Side A's attacks were ordered by Charpentier, chief of the general staff, and by Masséna through Solignac (claim side-a-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Koch, as in claims koch-side-a and side-a-command; Angeli, as in claims side-b-command and angeli-side-a; the demonstration as in claims angeli-side-b and koch-side-b.

claims.value: The passages read place side B on the heights of Fojano (Angeli) and at Ca Albertini (Koch), with 2 companies at S. Anna, and side A's men in the château San Felice, Seras's detachment sent by Parona and San Rocco and Solignac's column sent into the val Pantena; they name no works from which side B fought. The one work named is the château San Felice: Koch says the 22nd, too inferior in number, was thrown back onto its breaches, and Verdier gathered the men he met in the château and moved against the enemy; he does not say either side fought from it.
claims.rationale: Code none_named: no passage read has either side fight from works. The castle's breaches are named only as the place onto which side A's beaten regiment was thrown back, and the castle as the place where Verdier gathered men before moving against the enemy, so they are recorded here and not coded as side A fighting from works. none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. claims.value: Side A attacked. In Moriggl, Ney decided after Swinburne's refusal to take the place by force (OCR); on 4 November his troops stormed the fortress from 1 o'clock to ¼ past 5 in three general assaults, which were beaten off, while Loison's column turned and took the Leutasch work; after Loison reached Seefeld, French detachments pushed Swinburne's withdrawing column off the road, fell on its flank and forestalled it at the defile, where it surrendered after a short attempt to force the passage. In Victoires, Loison's division invested the Leutasch post, and on 5 November Loison's columns attacked the fort of Scharnitz, the 69th escalading it, and caught the evacuating garrison between two fires near a monastery.
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side A attack both posts and then trap side B's garrison as it withdrew, so the code is A_attacked; they agree on the code, so it is one claim. Swinburne's attempt to force the passage at Seefeld (Moriggl) and the Austrians' near success against the French first column (Victoires) were a withdrawing column's attempt to break through troops barring its way, not a main attack, so they do not make the code both_attacked. The passages show side A's commanders deciding the attacks: Ney decided to take the place by force (Moriggl, OCR), sent Loison against the Leutasch (Moriggl) and wanted to attack the Pass of Scharnitz (Victoires), and Loison directed the columns of 5 November (Victoires); so the posture is tagged commander_created. The invasion of the Tyrol was ordered by Napoleon (claim side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): as in claims side-a-command, side-b-command, bodart-winner, victoires-side-a and victoires-side-b.

claims.value: Side B fought from works. Moriggl's Scharnitz is a fortress whose garrison, well covered in the works, beat off the assaults, with Landesvertheidiger in the works, especially on the Kapfelberg; in his OCR the assaulting columns set ladders against the works. The Leutasch work, also called a fort, had a wall toward the Grünkopf and works in the plain held by the military. Victoires calls the Leutasch a fortified post and has the 69th escalade the walls of the fort of Scharnitz under fire from its ramparts. No works are named where Swinburne's column was caught near Seefeld.
claims.rationale: Code B_fortified: both accounts have side B defend the fortress of Scharnitz and the Leutasch work, permanent works in place before the campaign. In Moriggl's OCR the Leutasch work was walled, with bastions, a broad and deep wet ditch and a drawbridge, and a beam still standing bore a year that the OCR gives; so the fortification is tagged inherited. The accounts agree on the code, so it is one claim. Grueber's stone batteries on the Brunnstein were rocks prepared for rolling down the cliff, not works, and are recorded here only. Moriggl says a careful commander would have dug a cutting or a trench, raised a redoubt or laid an abatis at the Alpl, and that Kraus did none of this, so no field works are named there. Side A fought from no works. English renderings (ours): Moriggl, as in claim side-b-losses-reported for the dead covered in the works; as in claim scharnitz-ground for the Kapfelberg, the wall and the works in the plain; 'when the storm columns had pushed up to the works, the ladders were at once set up right and left and the storming went on' (OCR); as in claim moriggl-leutasch for the fort; 'it was solidly walled, had ... (OCR) bastions, a broad and deep wet ditch, over which a drawbridge led' (OCR); 'a beam of it still standing shows the year ... (OCR)' (OCR); 'further, a careful commander, such as perhaps a Swinburne, would have made a cutting here, thrown up a trench there, or built a redoubt, perhaps also had an abatis laid'; as in claim moriggl-leutasch for 'Major Kraus did none of all this'; as in claim scharnitz-ground for the stone batteries; Victoires, as in claims victoires-side-b and scharnitz-ground.

claims.value: Side A attacked. Davout reported that the advanced guard under General Heudelet met Merveldt's corps ahead of Neuhaus and that Heudelet attacked with the greatest vigour; the Austrians were broken and routed, and 5 companies of the 108th charged the enemy as he tried to rally at Mariazell. In Schönhals the French fell on the Austrian troops near Neuhaus and took their guns, seized houses below Zell, attacked again on both wings, stormed the castle of St. Sigmund and fired on the column in the defile; Merveldt's own attack near Neuhaus with troops he had gathered, in which the French were taken in the middle and one of their light battalions laid down its arms, and the detachments he sent against the French left flank at Mariazell were counter-strokes. In Alombert and Colin (OCR), the French carried the positions near Neuhaus and at Mariazell with charges.
claims.rationale: All three accounts have side A attack and side B stand, strike back and retreat. Merveldt's counter-strokes near Neuhaus and at Mariazell were made by the side retreating and defending, so the code is A_attacked, and as the accounts agree it is one claim. Heudelet, commanding the troops engaged, attacked without considering the enemy's numbers (Davout), so the posture is tagged commander_created; Davout's march orders are recorded in claim side-a-command. English renderings (ours): as in claims davout-side-b, side-a-engaged, side-a-command, side-b-command, side-b-information and bodart-winner.

claims.value: Both sides attacked. Mortier was preparing to attack on the morning of 11 November when Miloradovitch forestalled him, and the combat fell into two phases, Miloradovitch and Stryck in the morning and Doktorow in the evening. In their narrative (OCR), the Russians suddenly took the offensive and Miloradovitch attacked both in the small plain of Loiben and on the slopes; French light infantry battalions drove the enemy back into the wood, and a French charge threw the Russians back into Unter-Loiben; Mortier resolved to drive them out of Unter-Loiben for good. Danilewski's relation, which they find in close agreement with the French documents, has a French attack on the Russian right fail and Mortier finally drive Miloradovitch out of Loiben and pursue him to Stein; in the plain, therefore, the French success was final, though not in the mountains. In the evening Doktorow's advanced guard, having passed through Dürrenstein, deployed east of the town in a concentric attack on the division; on Mortier's order the grenadiers attacked into the walled road by which it advanced, and the Russian column broke up. Between Weissenkirchen and Wadstein a regiment that Dupont brought up beat the charge against Doktorow's column while the Russians came on with equal daring, and Doktorow, by Danilewski, was forced to clear the road and let Mortier pass.
claims.rationale: Code both_attacked: Alombert and Colin describe main attacks by each side, Miloradovitch's on Loiben, answered by a French offensive that drove him back to Stein, and Doktorow's on Gazan's rear, met by Dupont's attack between Weissenkirchen and Wadstein on another part of the field. The French were bivouacked, not holding a defended position, when they drove Miloradovitch to Stein, so the exception for a counterattack inside a defended position does not apply. Their account rests, by their own list, on French documents (a regimental colonel's letter to Berthier, General Graindorge's report on his artillery, the journal of Dupont's division and the notes in the return of the officers), on two partial Austrian eyewitness relations in the Vienna war archives and on Danilewski's Russian relation, and, with precautions, on Talandier's narrative and Rozat's fragment; there is no official French relation of the combat (OCR). Schönhals's account, coded separately, has only side B attack (claim posture-schoenhals). Both commanders decided to attack at this engagement, Kutusow in resolving to carry off Gazan's division and Mortier in preparing to attack and resolving to clear Unter-Loiben, so the posture is tagged commander_created. claims.value: Side B attacked. Kutusow decided on the evening of the 10th to attack the French the next day; at 7 in the morning Miloradović's division attacked the French advanced posts by the Danube, threw them back and occupied Unter-Loiben; the French, holding the slopes with guns, threw back the Russian right wing, forcing the troops by the Danube into a short backward movement, and not long after Ober-Loiben too was stormed. In the evening Schmidt's column came down behind Dürrenstein; the French made front against it, their cavalry's attempts to break through were repulsed, everyone advanced on the height where the French infantry stood, and 1000 men laid down their arms. In Schönhals's footnote after Kotzebue, Dupont's division ran into Schmidt's column at Wadstein and tried to break through, but, taken in flank and rear, had to re-embark and cross to Rossatz.
claims.rationale: Code B_attacked: Schönhals has side B attack throughout, and side A's repulse of the Russian right wing, its cavalry's attempts to break through and Dupont's attempt in Kotzebue's version are counter-strokes or attempts to escape by the side attacked. Alombert and Colin's account is coded separately (claim posture-alombert-colin). The passage does not say who stormed Ober-Loiben. By his footnote Schönhals took some details from Kotzebue for want of more reliable sources, and his editors call his account of the engagement meagre and incomplete for want of material, pointing to its description in their journal's volume for 1860. Kutusow decided the attack at this engagement, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): as in claim side-b-command for the decision; 'at 7 in the morning Miloradović's division attacked the enemy's advanced posts by the Danube. These were thrown back and Unter-Loiben occupied'; as in claim durnstein-ground for the slopes; 'and in fact they threw the Russians' right wing back again, and this circumstance forced the detachments fighting by the Danube too into a short backward movement; not long after, Ober-Loiben too was stormed'; 'it was 4 in the afternoon when the head of Schmidt's column came down through the ravine to the Danube about 2000 paces behind Dürrenstein'; as in claim schoenhals-figures for the French front; 'the latter at once made an attack in the flat vineyards on the wing leaning on the Danube and tried to cut its way through, but was repulsed by a violent musketry'; 'the Russian Jäger advanced skirmishing on the slope of the mountain, while the column following deployed and kept up the fire until dark, without advancing'; 'the fire of the French grew ever weaker'; as in claims side-b-information and side-b-losses-reported for the evening; footnote, 'according to Kotzebue, Dupont's division ran into FML Schmidt's column at about 4 in the afternoon at the moment when the latter arrived at Wadstein, coming down from Resch'; 'it tried to break through, but, taken in flank and rear, after a bloody hand-to-hand fight it had to re-embark and cross over to Rossatz'; as in claim schoenhals-figures for Kotzebue as a source; '[editors' footnote] the above account of the engagement at Dürrenstein has turned out meagre and incomplete for want of the material available to the author'; 'all the more as it was described in this journal, volume for 1860'.

claims.value: Neither account names works that either side fought from. Side A had passed the night in the basin of Loiben (Alombert and Colin, OCR), its division camped with the right wing at Ober-Loiben and the left on the lower slopes of the heights (Schönhals, OCR), with small posts on the neighbouring heights, which Alombert and Colin give with every reserve from Kotzebue (OCR), and pickets by the ruins of the castle and on the Neudeck (Schönhals). In the fighting side A held the plateaus above the villages, on one of which Fabvier defended his guns, and heights near the castle of Dürnstein (Alombert and Colin). Side B came down from the mountains, part of it through the little town of Dürrenstein, which Schmidt found unoccupied (Schönhals). The walls named are those of the vineyards and of the road to Dürnstein, along which the Russian column advanced in the evening and the grenadiers attacked it (Alombert and Colin, OCR, and the Austrian relation they quote), and the wall that joins the castle ruin above Dürrenstein to the town (Schönhals, OCR).
claims.rationale: none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. The vineyard and road walls are named as obstacles and as the setting of the evening fight, not as works either side fought from, and no passage read has either side defend the castle ruin or the town; if the walls of the road were counted as works, the evening fight on the road would code B_fortified. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim, and a none_named code takes the phase unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'our troops had passed the night in the basin of Loiben, in gloomy weather,' (OCR); Schönhals, 'the division camped with its right wing at Ober-Loiben, with its left on the lower, fairly steep slopes of the heights of the same name' (OCR); Alombert and Colin, 'we place small posts on the neighbouring heights, Pfaffenberg, Laken and Neudeck' (OCR); 'this last information with every reserve. It comes from the [attempt at a description of the battle at Dürnstein] of Captain W. von Kotzebue (... (OCR)), a very inexact work,' (OCR); Schönhals, 'by the ruins of the castle and on the ridge of the mountain, the so-called Neudeck, stood pickets, whose patrols came close to the Scheibenhof' (p. 135); Alombert and Colin, as in claim durnstein-ground for the plain and the plateaus; as in claim side-b-losses-reported for General Campana on the plateau (OCR); as in claim side-a-losses-reported for Fabvier on the plateau (p. 162); as in claim side-a-command for the plateau near Ober-Loiben (OCR); '[a regiment that had bivouacked behind Dürrenstein crossed the town ...,] detaching its ... (OCR) battalion onto the heights near the castle,' (OCR); '[Captain Laforest, ...] placed in observation on heights between the castle of Dürnstein and the regiment's left flank,' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the town found unoccupied; as in claims durnstein-ground, side-a-command and side-b-information for the vines and walls, the walled road and the fight between walls (OCR); the relation, as in claim side-b-losses-reported for the road (p. 162); Schönhals, as in claim durnstein-ground for the castle ruin (OCR).

claims.value: Side A attacked. In Moriggl, on 13 November the enemy attacked and pushed back the imperial outposts near Bregenz, and on the 14th French troops marched toward the Hohenems position, some detachments toward Staufen and the Bregenzerwald, and threw the Austrian outposts at Dornbirn out of the village and over the Dornbirner Ach, until Wolfskehl had the firing stopped; side B then capitulated. In Victoires, Augereau forced the Austrians to abandon Lindau and Bregenz and marched toward Feldkirch, and the Austrian general, soon surrounded, asked for a capitulation.
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side A advance on and surround side B, which capitulated without a battle; side B did not attack, so the code is A_attacked, and as the accounts agree it is one claim. Victoires says Augereau received the order to move onto the Vorarlberg to contain Jellachich's corps and push it onto the Tyrol (claim side-a-objectives). No passage read shows Augereau or Mathieu deciding at this engagement to attack: Moriggl names no commander for the attacks on the outposts or the turning detachments, and Augereau reached Bregenz only at noon on the 14th. So the posture is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): as in claims side-a-command, moriggl-side-a, side-b-command and side-a-objectives.

claims.value: In Moriggl, side B's main body stood in the position of Hohenems, into which Jellachich ordered the retreat on 5 November and where entrenchments were then built; Moriggl writes that Jellachich seems to have counted too much on this strong position, which could, however, easily be turned on the right side. His outposts were thrown out of the village of Dornbirn.
claims.rationale: Code B_fortified because a cited passage names entrenchments at the position side B held when it capitulated. The passages read describe no assault on them: French detachments moved to turn the position and the corps capitulated. No works are named where the outposts fought, near Bregenz and in the village of Dornbirn. The phase is left unresolved: the passages say entrenchments were built after Jellachich ordered the retreat into the position on 5 November, not on whose order or that they were built for this engagement. Side A fought from no works. English renderings (ours): as in claim side-b-command for the retreat into the Hohenems position, the strong position and the return of his men to it; as in claim moriggl-side-a for the turning detachments; as in claim side-a-command for the outposts at Dornbirn.

claims.value: Side A attacked. Murat ordered the attack on the Russian position behind Schoen Grabern (Victoires) or Schöngrabern (Schönhals): Oudinot's grenadiers attacked in front and on the left (Victoires) or against the Russians' centre and right wing (Schönhals), Legrand's division turned the position or attacked the Russian left, and Vandamme supported or followed in reserve. Side B held its position and received the attack.
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side A attack a position side B had taken and held, so the code is A_attacked. The French charge on the Russians who had cried out not to fire (Victoires, OCR) is part of side A's attack. Murat decided to attack at once, at nightfall, against Soult's advice (Victoires) and after Napoleon refused the convention, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): as in claims side-a-command, side-b-command and side-b-losses-reported.

claims.value: Both sides attacked. Side A moved against side B: St. Cyr advanced against the approaching enemy (Angeli) and Reynier was ordered to march on Castel Franco (Koch). Side B attacked: Rohan forestalled the attack and threw himself on Reynier's division, returning to the charge several times (Koch), and the Austrians tried for several hours to break through side A's lines (Angeli). Meanwhile side A turned and enveloped side B: the Poles turned Rohan, and the rout ran back to Castel Franco (Koch); surrounded on all sides, the Austrians laid down their arms (Angeli).
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side B attack to break through and side A advance against it and envelop it, so the code is both_attacked. Reynier's division received Rohan's attack and repulsed it, which by itself would be defence; the Poles' turning movement and the pursuit into Castel Franco (Koch) and side A's advance and encirclement (Angeli) are attacks outside any defended position. Each side's commander at the engagement decided to attack, Rohan to forestall side A's attack and St. Cyr to advance on the first news of the enemy, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): as in claims side-a-command, side-b-command, angeli-side-a, angeli-side-b and bodart-winner.

Side A attacked the allied centre: Soult advanced Saint-Hilaire's division to attack the heights and village of Pratzen, and Kutusow found himself attacked when he believed himself the attacker (Victoires, OCR); in Schönhals Napoleon gave the order to attack when the fog lifted, and the enemy's quick and unexpected attack thwarted the allied plans (OCR). On the allied right Bagration attacked the santon position (Victoires, OCR) or ordered a general advance of his corps (Schönhals, OCR).
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side B attack under its disposition, from the page images (Victoires p. 239; Schönhals p. 156), and side A attack the allied centre on the Pratzen heights, in the OCR (Victoires pp. 243-245, 247, 250 and 258; Schönhals pp. 159, 161, 163 and 165); the code is both_attacked. claims.value: Side A fortified the santon, a position from which it fought: Napoleon had the height on which Lannes's left rested fortified and occupied with all the more care because he regarded it as the key of his offensive operations; eighteen guns were placed there in battery, and the seventeenth light infantry regiment under General Claparède of Suchet's division held it. Bagration attacked it without yet knowing its strength, and the French artillery soon forced the Russians back to Posorzitz (Victoires, OCR); in Schönhals, Bagration's general advance brought on a murderous cannonade, which the enemy kept up with the greater success from his commanding position because the Russian batteries stood lower (OCR). Schönhals has the village in front of Lannes's wing occupied with guns and a light infantry regiment under Claparède (OCR) and does not call it fortified. Before the battle Napoleon had retrenchments built with much show and garnished with artillery on the heights his advance guard then crowned, as if he meant to keep them (Victoires, OCR); in its account he later withdrew his outposts to Telnitz, Sokolnitz and Schlapanitz (OCR), and the passages read do not say that those works were used in the battle. At Telnitz the French infantry fought from the ditch that surrounded the village like an entrenchment (Schönhals, OCR), a ditch bordering the vines that Victoires calls a natural retrenchment (OCR). No passage read names works on side B's side.
claims.rationale: Code A_fortified: Victoires's page image says Napoleon had the santon fortified and occupied, with eighteen guns in battery, and both accounts have side B attack the position (OCR). The retrenchments built for show before the battle and the ditch at Telnitz are recorded but do not decide the code: the former stood on heights the French then gave up, by Victoires's account, and the latter is a ditch of the village, which Victoires calls a natural retrenchment. The santon's works were Napoleon's choice, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Victoires, as in claim austerlitz-ground for the santon; 'eighteen pieces of cannon were placed there in battery, and it was guarded by the seventeenth regiment of light infantry, under the orders of General of Brigade Claparède, of the division Suchet' (p. 238); 'that famous position of the santon of which we have already spoken, defended by eighteen pieces of cannon, and guarded by the seventeenth light infantry, under the orders of General Claparède' (p. 258, OCR, its figures as on the p. 238 image); as in claim side-b-command for Bagration's attack; 'the French artillery, firing with liveliness and precision on the Russian troops, soon forced them to fall back as far as Posorzitz' (p. 258, OCR); as in claim side-b-information for the retrenchments and the outposts; '[nature had] formed a natural retrenchment around the village; the vines were bordered by a ditch in which the French held themselves as in a covered way' (p. 245, OCR); Schönhals, 'there now arose a murderous cannonade, which, however, was kept up on the enemy's side from his commanding position with overwhelming success, since the Russian batteries stood lower' (p. 165, OCR); 'in front of it, it had the village of TwaroJna (so the OCR), which was occupied with ... (OCR) guns and the ... (OCR) light infantry regiment under the command of General Claparède' (p. 158, OCR); 'the enemy had thrown his infantry into the ditch that surrounded the village like an entrenchment' (p. 159, OCR).

claims.value: Side B attacked. Both accounts have the Austrians make the general attack on 5 December: Völderndorff an hour and a half after noon, Schönhals in columns ready by noon, the left wing beginning. Side A held its positions at Stecken and Wonau and on the heights behind, then fell back by order to Iglau, its Chevauxlegers charging the enemy in the town, the battalion Dietfurth driving off the attackers several times with the bayonet (OCR), and its cavalry at the Sandhöfe charging to cover the retreat (OCR).
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side B attack side A's positions, so the code is B_attacked. Side A's charges were made inside its defended position or to cover its retreat; they do not make side A an attacker on 5 December. Wrede's attack of 3 December (claim side-a-command) was a separate action. The Archduke decided the attack, so the posture is tagged commander_created. The fighting was with stubborn bitterness'; 'Count Rechberg recognised the destruction of his men if he quietly awaited the powerful enemy' (OCR); as in claim bodart-winner for the third attack.

citations.quote: Der Feind hatte bei Wonau, zu beiden Seiten der Strasse, eine starke Stellung bezogen, deren Flügel an fast undurchdringliche Wälder gelehnt waren.

record.dependency_note: Official history of the French army's Section historique (published 'sous la direction de la Section historique de l'état-major de l'armée'), by P.-C. Alombert and J. Colin, printed 1902-1908; not a record of 1805 itself, and the same family as tomes II and III already registered. It narrates and prints French orders, letters, reports and corps and divisional journals, so it is the French side's own record. Its preface says that many documents for this period were published in Alombert's own book on the combat of Dürrenstein (1897), to which the volume refers ('Alombert' with page numbers), and thanks the officers of the Vienna Kriegsarchiv for documents used for Dürrenstein. XV; and Rozat de Mandres's recollections; it rejects Kotzebue's account of 1807 for the fighting. Its introduction cites Schönhals once, in a footnote on Austrian movements at the end of October, and its account of Merveldt's march to Neuhaus follows Schönhals's closely without citing him, so for Austrian-side statements it may not be independent of Schönhals.

record.dependency_note: Retrospective history by Moriz Edler von Angeli, k.u.k. Oberst, written by its title page on commission from Archduke Charles's sons and grandsons and 'nach österreichischen Original-Acten'. Its numbered source notes cite the Feldakten (F. A.) of the Kriegsarchiv, Archduke Charles's original relation, his generals' reports, original loss returns and Archduke Maximilian's diary. It is the Austrian side's account of the Army of Italy in 1805 and an interested one, commissioned by the commander's family. French dispositions and strengths in it are second-hand. Bodart's 46,000 for side A at Caldiero (Angeli 45,000), his loss of 1,200 for side B at Verona (Angeli 1622 and 76), his 4,000 for side B at Pojano and his 12 squadrons for side A at Castelfranco (Angeli 8) are not Angeli's.

record.document_date_note: A retrospective narrative of 1850 that prints documents of 1805-1807 with their own dates as pièces justificatives (Republican calendar with Gregorian equivalents). The print year is not an event date.
record.dependency_note: Retrospective history of Masséna's campaigns by General Koch, written by its title page from the documents Masséna left and from those of the Dépôt de la guerre and the Dépôt des fortifications. It is the French side's account of the Army of Italy in 1805, written from its commander's papers and so an interested account. It prints French documents as pièces justificatives (the army's ordre de bataille of 18 October 1805, reports of Generals Duhesme and Molitor), so it is not independent of them. Austrian dispositions and strengths in it are second-hand. Angeli (1897) cites pages of this volume in his source notes for the actions at Verona, Caldiero, Pojano and Castelfranco (notes 52, 62, 63, 65, 66, 68, 76 and 95; page numbers read in the OCR), so Angeli is not independent of it for those actions.

record.archival_identifier: Internet Archive 1805ieachtzehnhu00krau; Brigham Young University, Harold B. Lee Library
record.document_date_note: A retrospective narrative of 1912; it prints or paraphrases Austrian orders, reports and returns of 1805 but each selected passage is narrative, so all sections have no document date. The print year is not an event date.
record.dependency_note: Retrospective history by Alfred Krauss, k.u.k. Generalmajor, written in 1911 (preface dated Wien, September 1911), an Austrian officer's critical account of the Austrian army's 'unhappiest campaign'. By his preface it rests on the orders and letters of Napoleon and his marshals and generals printed in Alombert and Colin's La campagne de 1805 en Allemagne, and on the files of the k.u.k. Kriegsarchiv, which he says are not free of gaps. It is therefore not independent of the French official history for French orders and movements, while for Austrian orders, relations and returns it is a second-hand account from Austrian files (for example the relation of FML Auffenberg and the report of Archduke Ferdinand of 8 October 1805, listed as Beilage 6). It is an interested account in the sense that its author argues lessons for the Austrian army.

record.dependency_note: Retrospective history of the 1805 campaign, with Tyrol in the foreground, by Alois Moriggl, early-mass priest at Zirl and member of the Ferdinandeum at Innsbruck, begun as a monograph on the French invasion at Leutasch and Scharnitz under Marshal Ney. Johann Baptist Pachmann, continued by parish priest Grün; Baron Dipauli's notes on 1805; Beno Voglsanger's memoirs; the autobiography of a cavalry officer who served at Ulm; the diaries of Anton von Hepperger, Johann Pusch and Colonel Markus Hibler; Lorenz Rangger's history of the defence of the land; statements taken from surviving riflemen and defenders; and original documents of the Innsbruck registry and estates' archive. record.dependency_note: Retrospective history of the 1805 campaign in Germany 'after Austrian original sources' by Carl von Schönhals, an Austrian general, written in 1831 for an archive and published from his manuscript by the editors of the Österreichische militärische Zeitschrift in 1873; the editors' note says Thiers and Rüstow wrote later, and some footnotes are theirs. His preface says the narrative rests on the diaries of individual officers, that sources on the strength and organisation of the troops are deficient, that good sources on Russian strengths and losses are lacking, that intelligence on the French army is unreliable, and that everything on the French army's operations is drawn from that army's bulletins. It is the Austrian side's account, an interested one; French and Russian strengths and losses in it are second-hand. For Merveldt's corps it cites his report to the Hofkriegsrath, and for Dürrenstein it takes some details from Kotzebue's account of 1807, for want of better sources by its own footnote. Alombert and Colin's tome IV cites it once and follows its account of Merveldt's march closely, so for Austrian-side statements they may not be independent of it.

record.dependency_note: Retrospective compilation of the French wars of 1792-1815 'by a society of soldiers and men of letters'; this is its fifteenth tome. It is the French side's account and an interested one, and Austrian and Russian strengths, dispositions and losses in it are second-hand. Its narrative of Hollabrunn and Austerlitz names few sources: it cites the official bulletin by name in a footnote on p. 211 (OCR), in the selected Hollabrunn section; it cites Savary's report once, on the young officers around the Russian emperor (p. 229, OCR); it says that the French loss at Austerlitz was estimated at the time from the reports of the corps (p. 267); and it quotes Napoleon's proclamations of the eve of the battle and of 3 December. Elsewhere in the volume it says that the official bulletin cited Heudelet's brigade, in its account of Mariazell, and that the official bulletins omitted Major Henriod's conduct, in a footnote to its account of Dürrenstein (p. 207, OCR). It is later than the bulletins of the Grande Armée and draws on them at least there; how far its narrative of these engagements depends on them was not checked.
